title: A Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The Amitabha Sūtra is the essential teaching the World-Honored One proclaimed without being asked, the profound sūtra praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, the wondrous Dharma of ultimate expedience, the supreme and sudden refuge. It is the most important scripture of the Pure Land school, called the first sūtra of the Pure Land, because in it Śākyamuni Buddha reveals the method of liberation that assures rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in this very life.

inline.s: Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the later Qin dynasty.

The Amitabha Sūtra is the essential teaching the World-Honored One proclaimed without being asked, the profound sūtra praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, the wondrous Dharma of ultimate expedience, the supreme and sudden refuge. It is the most important scripture of the Pure Land school, called the first sūtra of the Pure Land, because Śākyamuni Buddha here reveals
the method of liberation that assures rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in this very life —
faith, vows, and recitation of the Name, with single-minded, unconfused focus

. Moreover, this Dharma is praised with one voice by the Buddhas of all directions (including, of course, Amitabha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss). Those who deeply give rise to faith and understanding are surely protected and remembered by the Buddhas of all directions; those who practice as taught will certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The sūtra says: "(Among the various)

Buddhas as innumerable as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land, puts forth his vast and long tongue, covering the entire three-thousand-great-thousand world, and speaks truthful words: You sentient beings should have faith in this sūtra of inconceivable merit, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."
It also says:

"If there are good men and good women who hear this sūtra and uphold it, and who hear the names of these Buddhas, all these good men and good women will be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and will never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, Śāriputra! You should all believe and accept my words and the words of the Buddhas."

The method of liberation in this life: a way to put an end to birth-and-death and escape the three realms within this very life. Ordinary paths, in order to end birth-and-death and leave the three realms, must completely eradicate all afflictions, which is extremely difficult and almost impossible to attain in one lifetime. But if in this life one cannot put an end to birth-and-death, then because of the confusion of passing from one body to the next, no one knows in which life or kalpa one will again take up the bodhi path. Yet the Buddha-recitation method that the World-Honored One teaches here, so long as one attains single-minded, unconfused focus, will surely bring rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss at death and put an end to birth-and-death. And single-minded, unconfused focus is far easier than eradicating all afflictions; it is something that anyone, with correct method and sincere, persistent effort, can attain in this very life. Therefore "faith, vows, and recitation of the Name, with single-minded, unconfused focus" is a method of liberation in this very life, praised with one voice by the Buddhas of all directions. Those who deeply give rise to faith and understanding are surely gathered in and received by the Buddhas of all directions; those who practice as taught will certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Confusion of passing from one body to the next: forgetting upon being reborn.
In this sūtra, the World-Honored One especially teaches how to ensure rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss:
faith, vows, and recitation of the Name, with single-minded, unconfused focus.

In so doing he establishes the doctrinal framework of the Pure Land school. Therefore this sūtra takes "faith, vows, and recitation of the Name, with single-minded, unconfused focus" as the essential method of practice.

To recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the most simple, direct, and secure path to escape birth-and-death; and among the four kinds of Buddha-recitation, recitation of the Name is again the most simple, direct, and secure, praised by the ancients as "the shortcut within the shortcut (the shortcut of shortcuts)."

The four kinds of Buddha-recitation: First, recitation of the Name, single-mindedly calling the Buddha's name; second, visualization of the image, gazing upon the Buddha's image while reciting the name; third, contemplation of the mark, inwardly contemplating the Buddha's adorned and splendid marks; fourth, contemplation of true reality, contemplating the true marks of oneself and of all Buddhas, which are neither empty nor existent, both empty and existent, and in which mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are without distinction.

The most distinctive features of this sūtra are: praised by the Buddhas of all directions, protected and remembered by all Buddhas, a horizontal transcendence of birth-and-death, never falling back, and attainment of buddhahood in one lifetime.
Praised by the Buddhas of all directions.
The sūtra says:
(Among the various)

Buddhas as innumerable as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land, puts forth his vast and long tongue, covering the entire three-thousand-great-thousand world, and speaks truthful words: You sentient beings should have faith in this 'sūtra of inconceivable merit, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas'."
Protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
The sūtra says:

"If there are good men and good women who hear this sūtra and uphold it, and who hear the names of these Buddhas, all these good men and good women will be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and will never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Horizontal transcendence of birth-and-death.
Master Yinguang says:

"Why is chanting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the West called the method of horizontal transcendence? The ancients gave a simile to explain it: they compare ordinary beings, who are replete with delusion and karmic afflictions, to a worm born in the lowest section of a bamboo; and this bamboo stands for the three realms. For this worm to get out there are only two ways: one is vertical emergence, the other horizontal transcendence. Vertical emergence is boring up from below, breaking through each section in turn until the topmost section is broken and only then getting out. This compares to
(the simile)
practicing other methods, which require eradicating all affliction of views and thought before one can escape the three realms
(before one can leave the three realms and put an end to birth-and-death)

. Afflictions of view number eighty-eight kinds, and afflictions of thought number eighty-one grades, and so many grades are compared to the sections of a bamboo. The worm boring straight upward is called vertical emergence. For example, a sage of the first fruit, who has cut off the afflictions of view, must undergo seven lifetimes in the heavens and seven in the human world through long kalpas of practice before attaining arhatship and ending birth-and-death. The second fruit must likewise pass one life in the heavens and return once to the human world before reaching the fourth fruit. As for the third fruit, whose afflictions of thought in the desire realm are already exhausted, one must still gradually practice in the five heavens of No-Return before eradicating the afflictions of thought and attaining the fourth fruit. Only then is one counted a sage beyond instruction who has escaped the three realms. If one is of dull faculties at the third fruit, one must even be reborn in the four heavens of emptiness, ascending from the heaven of the infinity of space to the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception, before attaining the fourth fruit. This method of vertical emergence is thus arduous and long. Horizontal transcendence, on the other hand, is this worm not breaking upward through each section but boring a single hole sideways, and so coming out. Such a method is far easier than vertical emergence. Those who chant the Buddha's name are likewise. Though they have not eradicated the afflictions of view and thought
(the afflictions of view and thought)

, if they can be complete in the three provisions of the Pure Land — faith, vows, and practice — at the moment of death they can move Amitabha Buddha to come and guide them to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once there, in that pure land, the afflictions of view and thought are eradicated without being eradicated. Why? Because the land of the Pure Land is excellent and its conditions are strong, with no conditions that give rise to affliction. Thus one gains the three non-regressions, and continues on until one pierces the dust-like
(the dust-mote afflictions)
ignorance
(the afflictions of ignorance)
, and perfects the supreme bodhi
(attaining buddhahood)

. How direct and simple a matter this is! Therefore the ancients said: pursuing the Way through other gates is like an ant climbing a tall mountain; chanting the Buddha's name for rebirth is like a sailboat driven by a favoring breeze."
(From a Dharma talk given upon returning from Shanghai to Lingyan)

The three realms: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world of sentient beings who have the two desires of sexual appetite and food, including from the six heavens of desire above, through humans and animals, down to the hungry ghosts and hells. The form realm is the world of sentient beings who are free of the two desires of sexual appetite and food but still have a body of form, including the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas. The formless realm is the world of sentient beings who have no physical body but abide in mind-consciousness in deep and wondrous concentration, including the four heavens of emptiness (the heaven of the infinity of space, the heaven of the infinity of consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all realms in which ordinary beings transmigrate in birth-and-death, so Buddhist practitioners first take escape from the three realms as their goal.
The three non-regressions:

First, non-regression of position, in which the position attained through practice is not lost; second, non-regression of practice, in which the method one practices is not lost; third, non-regression of mindfulness, in which correct mindfulness does not regress. Afflictions of view and thought: the afflictions of views and the afflictions of thought. Afflictions of views are the delusions and errors of ordinary beings in regard to views, such as the five wrong views of self-view, extreme view, wrong view, view of attachment to views, and view of attachment to precepts and practices. Afflictions of thought are the delusions and errors of ordinary beings in regard to thought, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt. These two afflictions are the root cause of sentient beings falling into the three realms and suffering birth-and-death in vain; to cut them off is to be able to end birth-and-death and escape the three realms. The dust-mote afflictions: these are the afflictions of bodhisattvas. When bodhisattvas work to convert sentient beings, if they do not penetrate the countless dharmas as numerous as dust and sand, they cannot complete the work of teaching sentient beings — hence the name dust-mote afflictions. The afflictions of ignorance: these are fundamental ignorance, which obscures the true principle of the middle way; when completely eradicated, one becomes a Buddha.
Never falling back.
The sūtra says:
"Sentient beings born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are all avinivartaniya
(never regressing)
Attaining buddhahood in one lifetime.
The sūtra says:
"All these good men and good women will be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and will never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi
(no longer regressing, until the attainment of buddhahood)

The Amitabha Sūtra has two extant translations: one is The Sūtra of the Buddha's Teaching on Amitabha, translated by Master Kumārajīva in the Yao-Qin period, often called the Qin translation; the other is The Sūtra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Protection and Reception, translated by Master Xuanzang in the Tang dynasty, often called the Tang translation. Master Kumārajīva, responding to the disposition of his countrymen to prize conciseness, translated mainly for meaning, so the text is concise yet rich, exquisite and fluent. Master Xuanzang, in order to preserve the original as much as possible, translated word for word literally, accurate and complete, retaining the original terms with precise and detailed meanings, which avoids the faults of misinterpretation and fabrication — and this is crucial for study and practice. When studying the sūtra deeply, comparing the two translations against each other yields a deeper and more accurate understanding. For the commentary on the Tang translation, see
A Commentary on the Sūtra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Protection and Reception
Note: the headings in this text were added by the commentator and do not belong to the sūtra itself.

blocks.text: 1. The Fine Assembly of the Buddha's Companions

inline.s: Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at the Garden of the Benefactor of Orphans and the Trees of Jeta in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of monks numbering twelve hundred and fifty, all of whom were great arhats, well known to all.

This is what I (Ānanda) personally heard. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha was at the Garden of the Benefactor of Orphans and the Trees of Jeta in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of monks numbering twelve hundred and fifty, all of whom were great arhats well known to all.

Thus have I heard: this is what I (Ānanda) personally heard. This sūtra was recited by Ānanda, a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha, when the scriptures were compiled. Ānanda: his full name is Ānanda, one of the ten great disciples of the Buddha. He was the Buddha's cousin, born on the night when the Buddha attained the Way; later he left home under the Buddha and attended him for twenty-five years, serving as the Buddha's attendant. He was renowned as foremost in extensive learning, and many scriptures were recited by him at the compiling. The ten great disciples: the ten great disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, namely: Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers; Subhūti, foremost in understanding emptiness; Ānanda, foremost in extensive learning; Upāli, foremost in upholding the precepts; Aniruddha, foremost in the divine eye; Mahākāśyapa, foremost in the ascetic practice; Pūrṇa, foremost in teaching Dharma; Kātyāyana, foremost in debate; Rāhula, foremost in secret practice. The ascetic practice: the practice of casting aside the three attachments of robes, food, and dwelling. One who cultivates the ascetic practice must observe twelve rules, called the "twelve ascetic practices." At one time: at that time. Śrāvastī: the name of an ancient kingdom in central India, also transliterated as Sāvatthi, located in what is now northwestern India, on the southern bank of the Rapti River. The Garden of the Benefactor of Orphans and the Trees of Jeta: this is a garden in Śrāvastī where Śākyamuni Buddha expounded this sūtra. Monk: one who has left home and received full ordination; a man is called a bhikṣu, a woman a bhikṣuṇī. Great monks: an expression describing that these monks were all of high attainment. Together: all gathered. Well known to all: known to everyone.

Led by these great arhats were: the elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Revata, Cūḍapanthaka, Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, Gavāṃpati, Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja, Kālodayin, Mahākapphina, Bakkula, Aniruddha, and all these great disciples.

The elder Śāriputra: "elder" means a monk of years and high virtue; "Śāriputra" is one of the ten great disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, renowned as foremost in wisdom. Mahā: a Sanskrit sound, translated in Chinese as great. Mahāmaudgalyāyana: that is, the great Maudgalyāyana, "great" added to distinguish him from another disciple surnamed Maudgalyāyana.
And likewise the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: Mañjuśrī, the Prince of Dharma, Ajita Bodhisattva, Gandhahastī
(qián)
Bodhisattva, and Nitya-praśānta Bodhisattva, together with all these great bodhisattvas.
There were also all the great bodhisattvas: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Gandhahastī Bodhisattva, and Nitya-praśānta Bodhisattva, together with all these great bodhisattvas.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattva: a Sanskrit sound, translated in Chinese as great bodhisattva. Mañjuśrī, the Prince of Dharma: that is, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Ajita Bodhisattva: that is, Maitreya Bodhisattva.
And likewise Śakra, lord of the gods, together with the countless gods of all the heavens.
And also Śakra and the countless gods of all the heavens came to the assembly.
Śakra, lord of the gods: also called Indra, lord of the second heaven (the heaven of the Thirty-three).

blocks.text: (1) What Is Meant by Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: At that time the Buddha said to the elder Śāriputra: To the west from here, passing through a hundred thousand koṭīs of Buddha-lands, there is a world called the Land of Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is now preaching the Dharma. Śāriputra! Why is that land called the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Because the sentient beings of that nation are free from all suffering and experience only happiness — therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

At that time, the Buddha told the elder Śāriputra: from here toward the west, passing through a hundred thousand koṭīs of Buddha-lands, there is a world called the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Buddha of that world is named Amitabha, who is now preaching the Dharma. Śāriputra! Why is that Buddha-land called the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Because the sentient beings there are free from all suffering and have only all manner of happiness — therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Buddha-land: the territory over which a single Buddha teaches. Sentient beings: here it means all living beings. World-Honored One: an honorific title for the Buddha, because the Buddha is honored by all people in the world.

blocks.text: (2) The Splendor of the Dependent Retribution

inline.s: Dependent retribution: the karmic reward upon which sentient beings dwell, such as the land, the earth, buildings, and furnishings — that is, the environment of one's life.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of netting, and seven tiers of trees, all made of the four treasures, and wholly surrounding it — therefore that land is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss, everywhere are seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of netting, and seven tiers of trees, surrounding it on all sides. They are all made of the four treasures, exquisitely beautiful — therefore that land is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Railings: balustrades. "Railing" refers to the horizontal rail; "shǔn (
shǔn/dùn

)" refers to the vertical rail. Netting: the netting of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with gold threads, pearls, and a hundred thousand varied gems, with jeweled bells hanging on all four sides, radiant in color and splendor, spread over the jeweled trees. The jeweled nets emit light, and within the light appear the images of the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; whichever land one thinks of in the mind appears of itself accordingly. Rows of trees: trees arranged in ordered rows.
Seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of netting, seven tiers of trees:
the railings surround the trees, and the exquisite jeweled nets cover the trees, layer upon layer alternating, their number being seven. The Sūtra of the Immeasurable Life of the Buddha says:

"Immeasurable jeweled nets spread over the Buddha-land, all made of gold threads, true pearls, and a hundred thousand varied gems, wondrous and rare, adorned and embellished, hanging jeweled bells on all four sides, radiant in color and dazzling, utterly magnificent. A naturally virtuous breeze arises softly and stirs gently. That breeze is harmonious, neither cold nor hot, mild and soft, neither slow nor swift. It blows through the jeweled nets and the many jeweled trees, producing immeasurable subtle sounds of Dharma, spreading a hundred thousand kinds of gentle and fragrant virtue. Those who hear them — their dust of toil and habits of defilement naturally do not arise. When the wind touches their bodies, they all gain bliss, like a monk who attains the concentration of cessation."
The four treasures: gold treasure, silver treasure, vaidūrya treasure, and sphatika treasure. Surrounding it on all sides: "circuit," to go around; making one full circuit is called one "circuit."

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds of seven treasures, filled with water of eight qualities of merit, and the bottom of the ponds is entirely laid with golden sand. On the four sides are steps and paths, made of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal. Above are pavilions and towers, also adorned with gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, conch-shell, red pearls, and agate. In the ponds are lotus flowers as large as carriage wheels, blue ones radiating blue light, yellow ones radiating yellow light, red ones radiating red light, and white ones radiating white light — subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such adornments of merit.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds of seven treasures, filled with water of eight qualities of merit, and the bottom of the ponds is entirely laid with golden sand. On the four sides are steps and paths, all made of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal. Above are pavilions and towers, also luxuriously adorned with gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, conch-shell, red pearls, and agate. In the seven-treasure ponds, the lotus flowers are as large as carriage wheels; blue lotus flowers radiate blue light, yellow lotus flowers radiate yellow light, red lotus flowers radiate red light, and white lotus flowers radiate white light — subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

Water of eight qualities of merit: this water has eight qualities — clear and pure, cool and refreshing, sweet and delicious, light and soft, moistening, serene and harmonious, allaying hunger and thirst, and nourishing all the faculties. Vaidūrya: a treasure like jade but translucent. Conch-shell (chē qú): according to the Expanded Materia Medica, Volume Forty-six, the conch is a large clam of the sea, with ridged markings on its shell like the tracks of a carriage wheel on the ground; the interior of its shell is white and smooth as jade, so it is often mistaken for jade. Later generations mostly use white coral and shells to make things called conch-shell. Red pearls: red precious jewels, exceedingly rare and precious. Adornments of merit: such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In that Buddha-land heavenly music is always playing, the ground is made of gold, and in the six periods of the day and night mandārava flowers rain down. The sentient beings of that land, at dawn, each take up fine flowers in their robes, and go to make offerings to a hundred thousand koṭīs of Buddhas in the other directions. At the time of the midday meal they return to their own land, and eat and walk, and so on. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such adornments of merit.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! That Buddha-land always has harmonious, elegant, and wondrous heavenly music, the ground is made of gold, and in the six periods of the day and night, mandārava flowers fall as though like rain. The sentient beings there, at early morning, each take up various fine flowers in their robes, and go to make offerings to a hundred thousand koṭīs of Buddhas in the other directions. At the time of the morning meal (breakfast), they return to their own land, and then eat, walk in meditation, and so on. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

The six periods of the day and night: ancient India divided a day and night into six periods: early day, middle day, late day, early night, middle night, and late night. Raining mandārava flowers: raining heavenly mandārava flowers as though from the sky; "flower" is the old word for "flower." Robe-jū (
gāi
): the lower hem of a long robe. Offering: the meaning of presenting and honoring. Meal: to eat; here "meal" is used as a verb. In the Sūtra of the Immeasurable Life it describes it thus:

"When one wishes to eat, bowls of seven treasures naturally appear before one. Gold, silver, vaidūrya, conch-shell, agate, coral, amber, moonstones, true pearls — such bowls come of their own accord. A hundred flavors of fine food naturally fill them. Though there is this food, there is in fact no one who eats; one only sees the forms and smells the fragrance, and conceives of it as food, and is naturally satisfied. Body and mind become soft and at ease, with no clinging to flavor; the matter passes away, and when the time comes it appears again."

Walking meditation: walking in a circle round a fixed place, cultivating concentration in the midst of movement. In this way one cultivates both motion and stillness, adjusting body and mind, and also avoids the dullness or drowsiness that comes from sitting long. Eating and walking meditation: the text speaks only of eating and walking, which is an abbreviated expression, "eating" standing for the activities of life and "walking meditation" for the deeds of practice.

Moreover, Śāriputra! In that land there are always all kinds of wondrous birds of various colors: white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and two-headed birds. These many birds, in the six periods of the day and night, produce harmonious and elegant sounds, and their sounds proclaim the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas. When the sentient beings of that land hear these sounds, they all recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Saṃgha.

Moreover, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are always all kinds of wondrous, brightly colored birds: white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and two-headed birds. These many birds, in the six periods of the day and night, produce harmonious and elegant sounds, proclaiming the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas. When the sentient beings of that land hear these sounds of Dharma, they all single-mindedly recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Saṃgha.

The two-headed bird: a bird with one body and two heads. The five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of effort (also called the faculty of diligence), the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. "Faculty" means root or foundation; these five faculties are the roots from which all wholesome dharmas grow. The five powers: the power of faith, the power of effort (also called the power of diligence), the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. When the five faculties gradually grow, they produce power — this is the five powers. The seven factors of enlightenment: "enlightenment" is bodhi; the "seven factors of enlightenment" are seven kinds of awakening: choosing the Dharma (the ability to choose the true Dharma), effort, joy (the joy that arises on attaining wholesome dharmas), tranquility, mindfulness (maintaining right mindfulness), and concentration. The seven factors of enlightenment are obtained through the five faculties and the five powers. The eightfold noble path: the eightfold noble path is also called the "eight right paths," a method of practice made up of eight mutually related parts: First, right view, which is correct understanding. Second, right thought, which is correct thinking. Third, right speech, which is proper words. Fourth, right action, which is proper conduct. Fifth, right livelihood, which is a proper occupation or way of life. Sixth, right effort, which is proper exertion. Seventh, right mindfulness, which is correct recollection. Eighth, right concentration, which is correct meditation. This method of practice is sacred because anyone who walks this noble path will surely become a noble one, distancing himself from suffering and affliction and passing beyond birth-and-death.

Śāriputra! Do not think that these birds are actually born as retribution for offenses. Why? Because in that Buddha-land there are no three evil destinies. Śāriputra! In that Buddha-land there is not even the name of evil destinies, how much less the reality? These many birds are all transformations made by Amitabha Buddha, in order to let the sounds of Dharma flow forth.

Śāriputra! Do not think that these birds are all born as retribution for offenses. Why? Because the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no three evil destinies. Śāriputra! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is not even the name of evil destinies — how could there really be beings of evil destinies? These many birds are all transformations Amitabha Buddha made by his power, in order to let the sounds of Dharma flow forth, and they have no consciousness.

The three evil destinies: the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals. These are the lower three destinies among the six destinies (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and gods). Sentient beings, from beginningless time, transmigrate within these six destinies.

Śāriputra! In that Buddha-land, the gentle wind moves the various jeweled trees and the jeweled nets, producing subtle and wondrous sounds, as if a hundred thousand kinds of music were all playing at once. Those who hear these sounds naturally all give rise to the mind of recollecting the Buddha, recollecting the Dharma, and recollecting the Saṃgha. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such adornments of merit.

Śāriputra! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the gentle wind moves the various jeweled trees and the jeweled nets, producing subtle and wondrous sounds, as if a hundred thousand kinds of music were being played at the same time. Hearing these beautiful sounds, one naturally gives rise to the mind of recollecting the Buddha, recollecting the Dharma, and recollecting the Saṃgha. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

blocks.text: (3) The Splendor of the Proper Retribution

inline.s: Proper retribution: the bodies and minds of Buddhas and sentient beings; this is the proper karmic reward obtained in accordance with past karmic causes.

Śāriputra! What do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitabha? Śāriputra! The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction — therefore he is called Amitabha. Furthermore, Śāriputra! The lifespan of that Buddha and of his people is immeasurably, boundlessly many asaṃkhyeya kalpas — therefore he is called Amitabha.

Śāriputra! How do you conceive of it? For what reason is the Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss called Amitabha? Śāriputra! The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction — therefore he is called Amitabha. Furthermore, Śāriputra! The lifespan of that Buddha and of his people is immeasurably, boundlessly many asaṃkhyeya kalpas — therefore he is called Amitabha.

What do you think: how do you conceive of it? Amitabha: translated in Chinese as immeasurable. This is because the Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss has immeasurable light, and the lifespan of that Buddha and his people is also immeasurable — therefore he is called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light (Amitabha Buddha). The lifespan of that Buddha and of his people, immeasurably, boundlessly many asaṃkhyeya kalpas: the lifespan of Amitabha Buddha and his people is immeasurably, countlessly many great kalpas. The Tang translation says:
"Śāriputra, because that Tathāgata and the sentient beings there have a lifespan of immeasurable, countless great kalpas."
An asaṃkhyeya
(qí)
kalpa: translated in Chinese as a kalpa of countless number. Countless: without end.

Śāriputra! Since Amitabha Buddha attained buddhahood, it is now ten kalpas. Furthermore, Śāriputra! That Buddha has immeasurable, boundless śrāvaka disciples, all arhats, whose number cannot be known by reckoning; the multitude of bodhisattvas is likewise. Śāriputra! That Buddha-land perfects such adornments of merit.

Śāriputra! Since Amitabha Buddha attained buddhahood, it is now ten kalpas. Furthermore, Śāriputra! Amitabha Buddha has immeasurable, boundless śrāvaka disciples, all arhats, whose number cannot be known by reckoning; and Amitabha Buddha's bodhisattva disciples are likewise, immeasurable and boundless, beyond the knowledge of reckoning. Śāriputra! That Buddha-land perfects such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

Śrāvaka: one of the ten dharma-realms (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas). An arhat is the highest fruit among the śrāvaka realm. Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas are called the four noble paths, no longer transmigrating in birth-and-death. Beyond the knowledge of reckoning: this cannot be known by counting.
Question: Are there women in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West?
Answer: There are no women in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West. The Sūtra of the Buddha's Teaching on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Awakening (a Chinese translation) says:
"In that land
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West)
are all bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and their lifespans are extremely long, without number of kalpas. Women who are reborn there are transformed and born all as men."
The Sūtra of the Buddha's Teaching on Amitabha's Three Kinds of Buddha, the Wonderful Dharma and the Path Across the Realm of Humans says:

"The second vow: when I attain buddhahood, let there be no women in my land. Women who wish to come and be born in my land will be born as men. The countless gods and humans, and the winged and creeping creatures of every kind, who come to be born in my land, are all transformed and born within the lotus flowers of the seven-treasure ponds. When grown they all become bodhisattvas and arhats, all without number. Only upon attaining this vow will I become a Buddha; if I do not attain this vow, in the end I will not become a Buddha."
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu's Treatise on Rebirth says:
"In the realm of Mahāyāna roots, there is no name even of reproach: women, the handicapped, and the two-vehicle species are not born there; whatever beings rejoice in, everything can be fulfilled."
Master Yinguang says:
"The Land of Ultimate Bliss has no women. Women, and animals, born in that world are all in the form of young men, born by transformation in the lotus."
(From the Collected Letters of Master Yinguang, Third Compilation
Letter One to the Layman Ye Fubei)

Furthermore, Śāriputra! Those born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are all avinivartaniya (never regressing); among them many are bodhisattvas of one more birth, their number exceedingly great, beyond the knowledge of reckoning — it can only be expressed as immeasurable, boundless asaṃkhyeyas.
